metric.concurrency.method: Static language-design analysis of TypeScript's concurrency model (single-threaded event loop, async/await, Promises, Worker Threads) based on language semantics and inspection of readable micro-benchmark sources.
observations: TypeScript inherits JavaScript's single-threaded, event-loop-based concurrency model. There is no shared-memory multithreading in the language itself; true parallelism requires spawning separate Worker Threads (or Web Workers) with message-passing (structured clone / SharedArrayBuffer for shared memory).

async/await and Promises are first-class, well-integrated language/type-system features (Promise<T> is fully generic-typed), giving excellent ergonomics for I/O-bound concurrency and composing asynchronous pipelines with strong static typing of resolved values and errors.
No built-in structured concurrency or cancellation beyond library convention; AbortController is a runtime pattern layered on top, not enforced by the type system.

CPU-bound parallelism is comparatively weak: Worker Threads require explicit message-passing boilerplate, structured cloning overhead, and separate module loading, unlike native shared-memory threads with typed channels (Rust, Go, Java, Kotlin).

SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics exist for low-level shared-memory concurrency across workers but are unergonomic, unsafe (no compiler-enforced data-race protection), and rarely idiomatic in typical TS code.
No compiler-level data-race safety guarantees (contrast with Rust's Send/Sync) since there is no shared mutable state across the single-threaded model by default.
metric.concurrency.scoring_rationale: Scored 55/100: TypeScript offers excellent, strongly-typed asynchronous I/O concurrency (async/await/Promise) which is a genuine language-quality strength, but true parallel/CPU-bound concurrency is bolted on via Worker Threads with weak ergonomics and no compiler-enforced safety, placing it below languages with native structured concurrency and shared-memory safety guarantees (Go, Rust, Java/Kotlin coroutines) but above languages with no cooperative async model at all.

metric.ffi_interoperability_design.method: Static language-design analysis of TypeScript/JavaScript FFI model on Node.js runtime, informed by inspection of readable TypeScript micro-benchmark sources under template/programs/typescript/micro.
observations: TypeScript itself has no native FFI keyword or ABI-level interop; interop is delegated entirely to the underlying JS runtime (Node.js N-API/node-ffi, Deno FFI, or WASM bindings).

Calling native code requires either writing a native Node addon in C/C++ using N-API (a separate compiled artifact, not part of TS language semantics) or using a third-party FFI package (e.g. ffi-napi, koffi) that maps C signatures dynamically at runtime with no compile-time type checking against the native side.

TypeScript's structural type system and .d.ts declaration files give reasonable static typing quality for JS-side wrappers once a hand-written or generated .d.ts exists, but the FFI boundary itself is untyped/unsafe (raw pointers as opaque numbers/BigInt, manual marshalling of structs/buffers).
WebAssembly interop (via Emscripten or wasm-bindgen-style tooling) is ergonomically decent but still requires generated glue and is not a language-level construct.
No first-class syntax for calling into shared libraries directly (unlike Zig's @cImport or Go's cgo); all approaches go through the host runtime's C++ embedding API or third-party packages.
Async/Promise-based native call wrapping is idiomatic and composes cleanly with TS's async/await, a genuine design strength for interop ergonomics on the calling side.
metric.ffi_interoperability_design.scoring_rationale: Scored 58/100: TypeScript/JS has workable but not language-native FFI; interop safety and typing across the native boundary are weak (untyped buffers/pointers, manual marshalling), while calling-side async ergonomics and declaration-file typing are genuine strengths. This sits below languages with built-in typed FFI (Rust, Zig, Go cgo, Swift) but above languages with essentially no practical FFI story.
